pairs.new: This section covers 1,955 definitions of faithfulness and of related notions, quoted from 204 of the 217 papers in this site's literature map (below, "the map"). Each definition has a kind, which says what sort of definition it is: 681 are operational (they describe a test or a measurement), 369 are informal (a definition in words), 297 are criteria (necessary or sufficient conditions for a notion, or assumptions it rests on), 231 are failure modes (named ways in which faithfulness or a related notion fails), 211 are formal (mathematical) and 166 are taxonomies (they divide a notion into types). Each definition also has a stance: 1,244 are proposed by the paper itself, 483 are adopted from an earlier paper as they stand, and 228 are adapted from an earlier paper with changes.

pairs.new: Here faithfulness concerns whether the answer causally depends on what the stated reasoning says. Several interventions test this dependence: truncating the CoT, inserting mistakes into it, unlearning a step from the weights, and swapping in a counterfactual CoT. Replacing the CoT with filler tokens tests whether extra computation alone explains the CoT's benefit, while paraphrasing it tests whether that benefit depends on information encoded in the phrasing ([Lanham et al. 2023](./#p=lanham2023measuring); [Tutek et al. 2025](./#p=tutek2025measuring); [Paul et al. 2024](./#p=paul2024making)).

pairs.new: [Jia et al. 2026](./#p=jia2026faithfulness) split the requirement on a trace $(P,C,A)$ (prompt, CoT, answer) into three parts. *Sufficiency*: $H(A\mid C)$ is low, so little uncertainty about the answer remains once the CoT is known. *Completeness*: $I(P;A\mid C)\approx 0$, so that $C$ screens off $P$ from $A$ (once the CoT is known, the prompt adds almost no information about the answer); an unverbalized hint is a completeness failure, which ties this group to group 2. *Necessity*: perturbing $C$ changes $A$.
